indiaMissions/india-amy-carmichael/summa: Amy Carmichael (1867–1951), an Ulster-born missionary sent by the Keswick Convention, worked in South India for fifty-five years without returning home. From 1901 she sheltered girls at risk of dedication as temple servants (devadasis), and her community at Dohnavur, formalised as the Dohnavur Fellowship in 1927, grew into a large children's home, school and hospital. Her many devotional books made her one of the most widely read missionary writers of the twentieth century, while her methods and claims have been debated.
indiaMissions/india-amy-carmichael/story:
Amy Beatrice Carmichael was born in 1867 at Millisle, County Down, into a Presbyterian mill-owning family. In Belfast she started work among the ‘shawlies’, girls employed in the mills, and through Robert Wilson, a founder of the Keswick Convention, she absorbed Keswick holiness teaching on surrender and the ‘victorious life’. In 1892 she became the first missionary supported by the Keswick Convention's mission fund. After a short and unhappy period in Japan (1893–94) and in Ceylon she went to India under the Church of England Zenana Missionary Society, arriving in November 1895, and after language study in Bangalore joined the CMS missionary Thomas Walker in the Tirunelveli district.

Carmichael adopted Indian dress, stained her skin with coffee to pass in villages, and formed the ‘Starry Cluster’, a band of Indian Christian women — among them the widow Ponnammal — who travelled with her through the villages of the Tamil south preaching to women. Her first book, ‘Things as They Are: Mission Work in Southern India’ (1903), deliberately broke with the cheerful tone of missionary reports by describing hardness of heart, caste pressure and the sufferings of converts; mission supporters at first found it too bleak to publish.

On 6 March 1901 a seven-year-old girl named Preena escaped from a temple at Tiruvannamalai to which she had been given and found her way to Carmichael at Pannaivilai. Her account convinced Carmichael that girls were being dedicated to temples as devadasis and exploited sexually, and from then on she gave herself to rescuing children at risk. That year she settled at Dohnavur, a Christian village founded in the 1820s under Rhenius and named after a Prussian benefactor, Count Dohna. The first infants were brought in from 1904, and over the following decades the community took in hundreds of girls and, from 1918, boys as well. Children were brought up in family-like ‘nurseries’ under Indian ‘accals’ (elder sisters), with schooling, Tamil Christian worship and a strict, disciplined community life.

In 1916 Carmichael formed the Sisters of the Common Life, a group of Indian and European women committed to celibacy and service; in 1927 the work was formally constituted as the Dohnavur Fellowship, independent of any missionary society. A hospital, the ‘Place of Heavenly Healing’, was built from the late 1920s and served the surrounding villages. Carmichael never took a furlough and was known to the children as ‘Amma’. In 1931 she fell into a pit and was badly injured, and she spent most of her last twenty years as an invalid in her room, writing: she produced some thirty-five books of devotion, verse and narrative, including ‘Gold Cord’ (1932) and ‘If’ (1938), which shaped evangelical spirituality in Britain and North America.

Her work was controversial. Her claims about the scale of temple trafficking were questioned by some contemporaries, and she was accused of abduction; on at least one occasion she faced criminal proceedings over a girl she had hidden from relatives, which were eventually dropped. Critics saw Dohnavur as a closed world that cut children off from their families and culture, and Carmichael's autocratic leadership and refusal of outside oversight caused friction with the CMS and the CEZMS. At the same time her campaigning contributed to public pressure against temple dedication, which the Madras legislature outlawed in the Madras Devadasis (Prevention of Dedication) Act of 1947, months after independence.

Carmichael died at Dohnavur on 18 January 1951 and was buried in the community garden under a bird-bath marked simply ‘Amma’. After her death the Fellowship passed gradually into Indian leadership and continues as an Indian-led body, caring for girls and elderly members of the family, running schools and a hospital. Elisabeth Elliot's biography ‘A Chance to Die’ (1987) made her a heroine of a new generation of evangelicals.

indiaMissions/india-amy-carmichael/legac: Amy Carmichael is among the best-known women in the history of missions in India, remembered for her devotion, her refusal to return home and her protection of vulnerable children. Historians also note the paternalism of her community, the separation of children from their families and her stark portrayal of Hinduism. Dohnavur survived her because Indian women had always done much of the work, and it continues under Indian leadership.

indiaMissions/india-indian-thinkers/summ: From the 1830s converts from high-caste Hindu and Sikh backgrounds began to interpret Christ in Indian categories: Krishna Mohan Banerjea read the Vedas as preparation for the gospel, Nehemiah Goreh refuted Hindu philosophy from within, Brahmabandhab Upadhyay tried to be a ‘Hindu-Catholic’ using Vedanta, Narayan Vaman Tilak wrote Marathi bhakti hymns, Sadhu Sundar Singh lived as a Christian sannyasi, and the Madras ‘Rethinking group’ (1938) challenged missionary forms of the church. Together they laid the foundations of Indian Christian theology.
indiaMissions/india-indian-thinkers/stor:
The first generation of Indian Protestant intellectuals came from Alexander Duff's English school in Calcutta. Krishna Mohan Banerjea, a Kulin Brahmin radical of the Young Bengal circle, was baptised in 1832 and ordained an Anglican priest; in ‘The Arian Witness’ (1875) and later works he argued that the Vedic sacrifice of Prajapati foreshadowed Christ, an early ‘fulfilment’ theology. Nehemiah (Nilakantha) Goreh, a Chitpavan Brahmin from Benares baptised in 1848, wrote ‘A Rational Refutation of the Hindu Philosophical Systems’ (1862), joined the Anglican Society of St John the Evangelist, and influenced the conversion of Pandita Ramabai. Outside the churches, Rammohun Roy's ‘Precepts of Jesus’ (1820) and Keshub Chunder Sen's lectures on the ‘Oriental Christ’ showed Hindu reformers admiring Jesus while rejecting the missions.

Brahmabandhab Upadhyay (born Bhabani Charan Banerji, 1861) moved from the Brahmo Samaj to Anglican baptism and then, in 1891, to the Catholic Church. Taking the dress of a sannyasi in 1894, he called himself a Hindu by birth and culture and a Catholic by faith, and in his journal ‘Sophia’ and hymns such as ‘Vande Saccidanandam’ he proposed that Advaita Vedanta could serve Indian Christianity as Aristotle had served Thomas Aquinas, with Brahman understood as Sat-Chit-Ananda (being, consciousness, bliss) and so as Trinity. His plan for a Catholic monastery (matha) for Indian ascetics was blocked by the apostolic delegate. Turning to nationalism, he edited the Bengali daily ‘Sandhya’ during the agitation against the partition of Bengal; arrested for sedition in 1907, he died in hospital before his trial ended. Rejected by church authorities in his lifetime, he later became a patron of Catholic inculturation and the ashram movement.

In western India Narayan Vaman Tilak (1861–1919), a Chitpavan Brahmin poet, was baptised in Bombay in 1895 and worked with the American Marathi Mission at Ahmednagar. He wrote hundreds of Marathi hymns in the abhang and other forms of the Varkari bhakti poets, which remain the core of Marathi Christian worship. In 1917 he gave up his mission salary to found ‘God's Darbar’, a brotherhood of baptised and unbaptised disciples of Christ, arguing that Indians must be free to follow Christ without adopting a foreign church. His wife Lakshmibai Tilak, who followed him into the faith after a painful separation, wrote the Marathi autobiography ‘Smriti Chitre’, a classic of Marathi literature.

Sundar Singh (1889–c.1929), born into a Sikh family at Rampur in Ludhiana district, had a vision of Christ on 18 December 1904 after burning a Bible in anger; disowned by his family, he was baptised in the Anglican church at Simla on 3 September 1905. He chose to live as a wandering sadhu in a saffron robe, preaching in the Punjab, the Himalaya and Tibet, and from 1918 to 1922 travelled through South India, Asia, Europe, Australia and America, where crowds saw him as an ‘Indian St Francis’. His teaching was simple, mystical and parable-filled; critics, including the Jesuit Father Hosten and the Swiss pastor Oskar Pfister, questioned the historicity of his miracle stories and Tibetan adventures, while Streeter and Appasamy's study ‘The Sadhu’ (1921) defended him. He disappeared on a journey into Tibet in 1929.

In Madras a group of lay intellectuals — the judge Pandipeddi Chenchiah, the lawyer and later mayor of Madras Vengal Chakkarai, and others including A. N. Sudarisanam, G. V. Job and D. M. Devasahayam — had formed the Christo Samaj (1919) to promote Indian Christian independence. When the International Missionary Council met at Tambaram in 1938, Hendrik Kraemer's preparatory book ‘The Christian Message in a Non-Christian World’ insisted on the radical discontinuity between the gospel and all religions. The group replied with ‘Rethinking Christianity in India’ (1938), arguing that the raw fact of Christ, not Western church dogma or institutions, was what India needed, that Hinduism could serve as an ‘Old Testament’, and that the church in India was too dependent on mission money and forms. A. J. Appasamy developed a bhakti theology of union with Christ in the Johannine writings and became a bishop of the Church of South India; Christian ashrams such as Christukula (Tirupattur, 1921) and Christa Prema Seva (Pune, 1927) tried to embody Indian forms of community.

After independence, P. D. Devanandan and M. M. Thomas, through the Christian Institute for the Study of Religion and Society (1957), turned Indian Christian thought towards dialogue with secular nationalism, Hindu renaissance and social justice, and later Dalit theologians criticised the earlier thinkers for drawing so heavily on Brahmanical traditions that most Indian Christians, who were Dalit or tribal, did not share. The pioneers nevertheless showed that Christianity could be thought and sung in Indian idioms rather than only translated from Europe.

indiaMissions/india-indian-thinkers/lega: These thinkers gave Indian Christianity its intellectual voice. They insisted that a follower of Christ need not become culturally Western and showed that Christian faith could be expressed through Indian philosophy, poetry and asceticism. Their dependence on high-caste traditions limited their appeal among the Dalit and tribal majority of Indian Christians, yet their questions about culture, the church and nationhood remain central to Indian theology.
